meta.description: Brolingo — A satirical dictionary of corporate buzzwords and the crimes committed against them.
meta.contributing: Add terms alphabetically within their category. Include all required fields. Be funny.

terms.part_of_speech: noun phrase (aviation metaphor for people who don't fly)
terms.corporate_definition: A broad, high-level perspective of a situation, deliberately stripped of details, nuance, or anything that might require actual knowledge.
terms.real_definition: Looking at the big picture. 'Let's take a 10,000-foot view' is how you say 'I would like to stop talking about specifics now.' At 10,000 feet, all problems look like someone else's problems.
terms.example: "Before we get into the weeds, let's take a 10,000-foot view." — We will remain at altitude for the duration of this meeting. The weeds will wait.
terms.brolingo_tip: At 10,000 feet, deadlines look like suggestions and accountability is obscured by cloud cover.

terms.corporate_definition: A list of tasks assigned at the end of a meeting that transforms accountability into a document nobody will read.
terms.real_definition: Things that should have been a Slack message. Often assigned to whoever stopped paying attention for 30 seconds.
terms.example: "Before we close out, let's capture our action items." — Person who will not follow up on the action items.
terms.brolingo_tip: If your meeting ends without action items, the meeting didn't exist. Add them retroactively for plausible deniability.

terms.corporate_definition: A software development philosophy that guarantees flexibility by replacing one rigid system with a different rigid system involving more sticky notes.
terms.real_definition: Moving fast in circles while generating documentation about moving fast in circles. The ceremonies: Stand-up (a meeting), Sprint Planning (a meeting), Retrospective (a meeting), Grooming (also a meeting).
terms.example: "We're fully Agile here." — Company with 47-step approval processes and bi-weekly Jira audits.
terms.brolingo_tip: True Agile practitioners can explain what a 'story point' is. No two will give the same answer.

terms.corporate_definition: A productivity methodology wherein an individual systematically delegates cognitive and administrative functions to generative AI to maximize personal output and optimize their life-stack efficiency.
terms.real_definition: The practice of asking ChatGPT what to have for breakfast, then asking it whether the breakfast was emotionally meaningful. AI-Maxxers don't make decisions so much as submit prompts about decisions, review the output, and iterate. They have optimized their calendar, their relationships, their morning routine, and their personality. The optimization has not made them better. It has made them faster at being exactly who they already were.
terms.example: "I asked Claude to optimize my morning routine." — It scheduled 22 minutes of intentional reflection. He now wakes up 45 minutes earlier and is significantly more tired than before.
terms.brolingo_tip: The logical endpoint of AI-Maxxing is prompting an AI to generate a better prompt for prompting the AI. Several people have already done this. They called it 'prompt engineering.'

terms.corporate_definition: The state of everyone nodding in a room while privately planning to do something different.
terms.real_definition: A meeting after a meeting to discuss what was decided in the meeting. Alignment is never achieved; it is only scheduled.
terms.example: "We need to get alignment on this before we can move forward." — Translation: One person disagrees and it's the wrong person.
terms.brolingo_tip: The more alignment a project requires, the less likely it is to ship.

terms.corporate_definition: A request, transformed into a noun to make the requester sound like they're doing you a favor by having needs.
terms.real_definition: A verb. The word is 'request.' Or 'favor.' Or just 'can you do this.' The word 'ask' is not a noun. It has never been a noun. It will never be a noun.
terms.example: "So what's the ask here?" — Person who has forgotten that grammar exists.
terms.brolingo_tip: Using 'ask' as a noun is the verbal equivalent of wearing a suit jacket over a hoodie. You're not fooling anyone.

terms.corporate_definition: A technical term for data transfer capacity, repurposed to describe human capacity without any of the measurability.
terms.real_definition: Whether someone has time. Just say 'time.' You can say the word 'time.' It is a perfectly good word.
terms.example: "Do you have the bandwidth to take this on?" — Prelude to assigning you something regardless of your answer.
terms.brolingo_tip: Unlike actual bandwidth, human bandwidth is always described as insufficient after the deadline has already been set.

terms.corporate_definition: Creative brainstorming unconstrained by reality, budget, physics, or the lessons of the last three times this was tried.
terms.real_definition: A meeting where bad ideas are welcomed right up until someone has to build them.
terms.example: "I want us to do some blue sky thinking on this one — no idea is too big!" — Person who will shoot down every idea.
terms.brolingo_tip: Blue sky thinking sessions are identifiable by the Post-it notes, the energy drinks, and the silence in stand-up the following Monday.

terms.corporate_definition: To attempt a task of impossible scope. Used as a warning, ironically, by the same people who assign the tasks.
terms.real_definition: An elegant way to tell someone their plan is too ambitious, usually in the same breath as assigning them a plan of equal ambiguity.
terms.example: "We don't want to boil the ocean here, but we do need to transform the entire customer journey end-to-end by Q3."
terms.brolingo_tip: If someone says 'we don't want to boil the ocean,' the ocean is already at a full rolling boil.

terms.corporate_definition: To revisit a topic at an unspecified future date that both parties understand will never arrive.
terms.real_definition: A socially acceptable way to say 'I do not want to answer this' or 'I have not done the thing I said I would do.' The meeting equivalent of 'leaving on read.'
terms.example: "Great question — let's circle back on that." — No one circles back. No one has ever circled back.
terms.brolingo_tip: The circle is not a loop. The circle is an exit strategy.

terms.corporate_definition: Describing a decision process in which data is consulted after the decision has already been made.
terms.real_definition: A qualifier applied to justify decisions using charts that support whatever the executive already wanted to do. The data didn't drive. It was put in the trunk.
terms.example: "We need to be more data-driven on this." — Phrase used when someone disagrees with your gut feeling and you need backup.
terms.brolingo_tip: Data is data-driven. Decisions are usually vibe-driven with a data-shaped garnish.

terms.corporate_definition: A thorough analysis, typically conducted in a meeting that is the same length as all other meetings.
terms.real_definition: A 30-minute Zoom call with a deck that has 47 slides. Depth is implied but rarely achieved.
terms.example: "Can we schedule a deep dive on the Q4 numbers?" — Calendar invite: 30 mins. Agenda: 'deep dive.' Outcome: TBD.
terms.brolingo_tip: In oceanography, a deep dive takes specialized equipment and days of planning. In business, it's a Thursday at 3pm.

terms.corporate_definition: A tangible output with a deadline, used to transform vague directives into slightly less vague directives.
terms.real_definition: The thing you promised two sprints ago that has since been redefined three times and is now technically on time because the definition changed.
terms.example: "What are the key deliverables for this phase?" — Great question to ask before the project starts. Usually asked after.
terms.brolingo_tip: A deliverable is only real once someone asks where it is.

terms.corporate_definition: Describing a product or company that does something that already exists but with an app and a startup blog post about it.
terms.real_definition: Originally meant to describe technologies that overturn established markets. Now means 'we have a mobile UI.' Uber was disruptive. Your B2B SaaS invoice tool is not.
terms.example: "We're a disruptive force in the enterprise loyalty space." — It's a punch card app.
terms.brolingo_tip: If you have to say you're disruptive, you are not disruptive. Disruption doesn't announce itself at a conference.

terms.corporate_definition: To examine an idea more closely by exploring its component details — typically deployed mid-meeting on a slide that was not designed for this level of scrutiny.
terms.real_definition: To zoom in. To ask a follow-up question, but with the confidence of someone who owns a standing desk. Borrowed from the literal act of double-clicking to open a file. Now used to mean: 'open this concept and show me what's inside, slowly, in front of everyone.'
terms.example: "I want to double click on the retention numbers for a second." — We will spend the next 25 minutes on this slide. The rest of the agenda is a suggestion now.
terms.brolingo_tip: A single click selects. A double click opens. A corporate double click opens a 45-minute discussion that may or may not close.

terms.corporate_definition: A company's product suite plus the products they depend on plus the products they acquired plus the products they wish they had.
terms.real_definition: A word used to make a collection of loosely integrated tools sound like a thriving natural wonder. In reality, it's three SaaS apps with a shared login page.
terms.example: "Our ecosystem of solutions enables end-to-end transformation." — Three tools. Two of them break when you update the third.
terms.brolingo_tip: Real ecosystems have biodiversity. Corporate ecosystems have vendor lock-in.

terms.corporate_definition: A self-reinforcing cycle in which early momentum compounds into exponential, unstoppable, paradigm-shifting growth — described confidently by someone who has not yet started the flywheel.
terms.real_definition: Things are going well. Or they should be going well. Or someone read 'Good to Great' on a plane and never fully recovered. The flywheel is momentum without a named source. Someone has to push it first. That someone is you. You are the flywheel.
terms.example: "Once we get the flywheel spinning, growth becomes self-sustaining." — The flywheel is not spinning. You will push it manually for the next three quarters while someone draws a diagram of it spinning.
terms.brolingo_tip: In mechanical engineering, flywheels store rotational energy. In business decks, they store optimism and Series A expectations.

terms.corporate_definition: Detailed. Very detailed. So detailed that you will be here for another forty-five minutes.
terms.real_definition: The word 'detailed' with a texture. Used to imply rigor without committing to it. 'Can we get more granular on this?' is a way of saying 'I don't understand what you just said.'
terms.example: "Can we get more granular on the data segmentation?" — Translation: 'Start over, but slower.'
terms.brolingo_tip: Sand is granular. Most corporate analysis is not. But calling it granular makes it sound like it is.

terms.corporate_definition: To generate ideas. The verb 'think' was apparently not impressive enough.
terms.real_definition: To think. To brainstorm. To have a thought. 'Ideate' is what happens when someone confuses syllable count with intelligence. It is not a word. It is a crime.
terms.example: "Let's ideate on some solutions here." — The word 'think' was right there. It was sitting right there.
terms.brolingo_tip: If you catch yourself using 'ideate' unironically, please take a moment to lie down in a quiet room.

terms.corporate_definition: A label applied to any product or process that was not available at this particular company approximately eighteen months ago.
terms.real_definition: Genuinely innovative things are not usually described as innovative by the people making them. They're too busy building. 'Innovative' is marketing. 'AI-powered innovative solution' is a checkbox in a form.
terms.example: "We're bringing an innovative approach to the accounts payable space." — They added a PDF export button.
terms.brolingo_tip: Every company on earth claims to be innovative. Statistically, this cannot be true.

terms.corporate_definition: An intensifier applied to nouns to signal importance, urgency, or relevance without providing any evidence of any of those things.
terms.real_definition: A magical adjective that can be placed in front of any noun to make it sound more important than it really is. Key learnings. Key stakeholders. Key deliverables. Key outcomes. Key takeaways. The word 'key' adds no information. It is the verbal equivalent of bold text.
terms.example: "What were the key learnings from our key stakeholders on the key deliverables?" — A sentence with three keys that opens no doors.
terms.brolingo_tip: Remove the word 'key' from any sentence and check if anything changes. It will not.

terms.corporate_definition: Lessons derived from an experience, typically a failure that no one is allowed to call a failure.
terms.real_definition: 'Learnings' is not a word. 'Lessons' is the word. 'Takeaways' is also the word. The word you want is 'lessons.' The plural of learning is lessons, not learnings, and yet here we are.
terms.example: "What were the key learnings from the pilot?" — The pilot failed. The learning is: it failed. Please say 'lessons.'
terms.brolingo_tip: Using 'learnings' is itself a learning about how language works. That lesson: don't do this.

terms.corporate_definition: To use a resource, relationship, or capability in a strategic way. Or just... to use something.
terms.real_definition: The word 'use.' Just use the word 'use.' 'Leverage our existing infrastructure' means 'use our existing infrastructure.' You are allowed to use the word use.
terms.example: "We can leverage the existing partnership to accelerate our go-to-market." — We can use the thing we already have to sell stuff.
terms.brolingo_tip: Leverage is a perfectly good noun (a lever's mechanical advantage). As a verb meaning 'to use,' it's just 'use' in a trench coat.

terms.corporate_definition: Easy wins that are always identified and never harvested.
terms.real_definition: The mythical easy tasks that will be prioritized next quarter, and the quarter after that, and the quarter after that. If the fruit is so low-hanging, why is it still on the tree in year three of the roadmap?
terms.example: "There's a lot of low-hanging fruit here we can go after first." — The fruit will remain on the tree. It has always been on the tree.
terms.brolingo_tip: The fruit is not hanging low. It is load-bearing. It cannot be picked without a six-month discovery phase.

terms.corporate_definition: To produce measurable progress, though the needle and its scale are never specified.
terms.real_definition: To do literally anything that produces a number that could be compared to a previous number. Which needle? On which gauge? Nobody knows. The needle is vibes.
terms.example: "We need initiatives that are actually going to move the needle." — As opposed to the other initiatives, which apparently moved nothing.
terms.brolingo_tip: No one has ever successfully defined where the needle starts or where it needs to end up. The needle is free.

terms.corporate_definition: The single guiding metric or vision that orients all company decisions. Typically defined in a 2-day offsite and forgotten by Friday.
terms.real_definition: A fixed point of reference. The problem: unlike the actual North Star, the corporate North Star moves every quarter and is usually redefined after the person who chose it leaves.
terms.example: "Our North Star metric is monthly active users." — Update: our North Star is now revenue. Update: our North Star is retention. Update: the North Star is a constellation now.
terms.brolingo_tip: Polaris is 323 light-years away and doesn't care about your OKRs.

terms.corporate_definition: How a situation appears to others — typically used to avoid discussing whether the situation is actually bad.
terms.real_definition: A way to talk about perception without discussing substance. 'The optics are bad' is the polished way to say 'this looks terrible and we're going to focus on that instead of why it is terrible.'
terms.example: "We need to think about the optics of this decision." — The decision was bad. We're not going to say the decision was bad.
terms.brolingo_tip: In physics, optics is the study of light and vision. In business, it's the study of what you can get away with.

terms.corporate_definition: Problems experienced by customers, partners, or employees that a product or initiative claims to solve.
terms.real_definition: Problems. The word is problems. 'Pain points' sounds more clinical and sales-forward, which is why it replaced 'problems' in approximately 2012 and has not left.
terms.example: "What are the core pain points we're solving for?" — What problems does this fix? Also: does it fix them?
terms.brolingo_tip: Calling them 'pain points' makes it sound like you have a solution. You may not have a solution. That's fine. Just say 'problems.'

terms.corporate_definition: A fundamental change in approach or underlying assumptions — or a minor process update presented as one.
terms.real_definition: Thomas Kuhn used this to describe a complete restructuring of scientific understanding (relativity, for example). You are using it to describe a new CRM rollout.
terms.example: "This isn't just an update — it's a paradigm shift in how we think about customer success." — They changed the ticket form.
terms.brolingo_tip: A real paradigm shift happens once per generation. Your fiscal year does not contain one.

terms.corporate_definition: Doing two or more things simultaneously, used to sound efficient while actually describing multitasking-induced chaos.
terms.real_definition: In computing, parallel execution means truly simultaneous processing by independent units. In corporate-speak, it means two teams are both doing the same thing without talking to each other.
terms.example: "Let's run those two workstreams in parallel." — Both will conflict, duplicate effort, and need to be reconciled in a two-day alignment session.
terms.brolingo_tip: Parallel lines never meet. Your workstreams absolutely will — at the worst possible time.

terms.corporate_definition: A strategic change in direction, typically rebranded from 'we ran out of money doing the first thing.'
terms.real_definition: Failing, but with a press release and a Medium post about 'listening to the market.' A pivot is only called a pivot if the company survives. Otherwise it's called 'the thing that happened before the shutdown.'
terms.example: "We're pivoting from B2C to enterprise." — Consumer users didn't pay. Also: the enterprise pivot will be announced in eight months.
terms.brolingo_tip: Startups pivot. Corporations 'strategically reorient.' Same thing. Both take six months to change a logo.

terms.corporate_definition: To transform a service, tool, or internal process into a sellable product offering.
terms.real_definition: This is usually said about a thing that was never designed to be a product, and the productizing will require rebuilding it from scratch. But 'productize' sounds faster than 'rebuild everything.'
terms.example: "We should productize our internal analytics dashboard." — The dashboard is a Google Sheet. The productizing will take eighteen months.
terms.brolingo_tip: The gap between 'productize this' and 'this is a product' is approximately: one full engineering team, six months, and two pivots.

terms.corporate_definition: To contact someone, expressed in a way that implies warmth and initiative.
terms.real_definition: To send an email. Or a Slack. Or a calendar invite. 'Reach out' replaced 'contact' and 'email' in the business vocabulary around 2014 and shows no signs of receding.
terms.example: "Feel free to reach out if you have any questions!" — Standard email sign-off. No one will reach out. Questions will fester.
terms.brolingo_tip: You can also just say 'email me' or 'message me.' The reaching is optional.

terms.corporate_definition: A strategic restructuring initiative designed to optimize organizational efficiency and unlock synergies across business units.
terms.real_definition: Something large companies do when they stop making as much money as they think they should. New boxes on the org chart. Same people, different reporting lines, fresh confusion. Doesn't usually affect most teams day-to-day other than a couple of weeks of pointless all-hands meetings and corridor speculation about who reports to whom now.
terms.example: "Following the reorg, our teams are better aligned to serve customer needs." — Dave now reports to Sandra instead of Marcus. Customer needs are unchanged.
terms.brolingo_tip: The primary output of a reorg is another reorg, typically 18 months later.

terms.corporate_definition: Sturdy, reliable, and resilient under load — typically applied to systems that have not yet been tested under load.
terms.real_definition: It worked in the demo. 'Robust' is what you call something before anyone has actually stressed it. Post-production incident, the preferred term is 'we're looking into some stability issues.'
terms.example: "We've built a robust, scalable architecture." — The architecture will require emergency maintenance next Tuesday.
terms.brolingo_tip: A thing described as robust before launch is rarely robust after launch. The word 'robust' is load-bearing in pitch decks.

terms.corporate_definition: The amount of time a company can operate before running out of money, measured in months and discussed in hushed tones.
terms.real_definition: How long until the layoffs. 'We have 18 months of runway' is a sentence that sounds optimistic and means exactly as much as it says: 18 months.
terms.example: "We have solid runway to hit our next milestone." — The milestone and the runway end at approximately the same time.
terms.brolingo_tip: Planes need runway to take off. Startups need runway to not crash. These metaphors share more than intended.

terms.corporate_definition: To grow a system, process, or business to handle increased demand — most often used before anyone has verified there is increased demand.
terms.real_definition: To do the same thing but more expensively, while calling it an achievement. 'Scale' is the goal of every startup and the budget justification of every enterprise IT project.
terms.example: "We need to build this to scale." — We have 200 users. The architecture now costs $40k/month.
terms.brolingo_tip: Premature scaling is the startup equivalent of buying a warehouse before your first sale.

terms.corporate_definition: The process of sharing an idea with stakeholders before formally proposing it, to build support through informal channels.
terms.real_definition: Pre-lobbying. 'Let's socialize this idea' means 'let's tell everyone individually so the meeting is just a formality and no one can object on record.' Not to be confused with socializing, which is the thing we miss.
terms.example: "We should socialize this with leadership before we bring it to the table." — We need buy-in. We will get buy-in. Resistance is futile.
terms.brolingo_tip: In sociology, socialization is how children learn social norms. In offices, it's how decisions avoid scrutiny.

terms.corporate_definition: Anyone with an interest in a project's outcome, including people who have never heard of the project but will have opinions about it.
terms.real_definition: Anyone who can say no. A stakeholder's power is inversely proportional to their involvement in the actual work. The more removed from execution, the more influential the stake.
terms.example: "Have you looped in all the stakeholders?" — There are seventeen stakeholders. Three of them are on vacation. One of them will veto the whole thing in week eight.
terms.brolingo_tip: In medieval times, a stakeholder literally held stakes. Those stakes kept things in the ground. Corporate stakes do the same thing to your project timeline.

terms.corporate_definition: The combined force of two teams that, when working together, should produce more than the sum of their parts — but in practice produces twice as many meetings.
terms.real_definition: The business case for merging two departments that were working fine separately. Synergy is always promised before a restructure and never measured after it.
terms.example: "The synergy between our teams will be transformative." — One team will absorb the other. This is the press release.
terms.brolingo_tip: In physics, synergy is a real phenomenon. In quarterly reviews, it is a number someone made up in a slide.

terms.corporate_definition: To move a conversation out of the current meeting into a smaller meeting, where it will be discussed until it can be taken offline again.
terms.real_definition: To table a discussion that is making someone important uncomfortable. 'Taking it offline' creates a new meeting to address the thing that should have been in the original meeting, and often a third meeting to follow up on the second.
terms.example: "Let's take this offline." — Translation: not in front of everyone, not now, possibly not ever.
terms.brolingo_tip: Taking things offline is the primary growth mechanism of the corporate calendar.

terms.corporate_definition: An individual recognized as an authoritative voice in their field, typically self-recognized, typically on LinkedIn.
terms.real_definition: Someone who has posted on LinkedIn often enough that people started agreeing with them. Thought leaders think thoughts and then share those thoughts. You can be a thought leader by having thoughts. The bar is low.
terms.example: "She's really a thought leader in the enterprise cloud space." — She has 40,000 LinkedIn followers and posts motivational content about 4am wake-up routines.
terms.brolingo_tip: If you call yourself a thought leader, you are not one. Thought leadership, like respect, is granted, not claimed.

terms.corporate_definition: Something that improves an offering beyond its baseline, used to justify any feature, service, or meeting's existence.
terms.real_definition: A way to describe something as useful without specifying how or to whom. 'This is a value add' means 'I believe this is good and I'd like you to agree without me having to prove it.'
terms.example: "The reporting dashboard is a real value add for our customers." — Customers have not used the reporting dashboard.
terms.brolingo_tip: Everything is called a value add. If everything adds value, the value has been added to nothing and therefore diluted back to nothing.

terms.corporate_definition: Industry sectors or market segments targeted by a company's products or services.
terms.real_definition: Markets. The word is markets. Or industries. Or sectors. 'Verticals' is the word for these things when you want to sound like you have a strategy for each one, even if the strategy is the same for all of them.
terms.example: "We're targeting three key verticals: healthcare, finance, and logistics." — The product is the same for all three. The sales decks have different stock photos.
terms.brolingo_tip: Verticals go up and down. Markets go in every direction. Semantics still matter, even if only barely.

terms.corporate_definition: In a competent, respectful, and business-appropriate manner consistent with workplace expectations and organizational standards.
terms.real_definition: Doing something while suppressing every natural human reaction you had to it. 'Professionally' usually means calm on the outside, composing an unhinged reply in drafts on the inside.
terms.example: "Please handle this professionally." — Please do not say what everyone else is already saying privately in Slack.
terms.brolingo_tip: The more urgently someone requests professionalism, the less professional the situation already is.

terms.corporate_definition: A complete reimagining of a business, product, or process — typically used to describe any change larger than a font update.
terms.real_definition: Change. The word is change. 'Transform' implies a caterpillar-to-butterfly situation. What you're describing is more of a caterpillar-to-slightly-different-caterpillar situation. But 'transform' sounds like the future, and 'change' sounds like admitting the past was wrong. So here we are.
terms.example: "We're transforming the way our customers experience support." — They added a chatbot. The chatbot does not work.
terms.brolingo_tip: Every transformation deck has a slide with a butterfly on it. The butterfly is not included in the budget.

terms.corporate_definition: To raise something to a higher level — typically the conversation, the brand, the experience, or the team's output.
terms.real_definition: To improve. But 'elevate' implies you're floating upward, which sounds better than 'fix the thing that's bad.' 'Elevate the conversation' means the current conversation is bad. 'Elevate the brand' means the current brand is bad. 'Elevate your game' means you specifically are the problem. All of these things have simpler words. None of them require a ladder.
terms.example: "We need to elevate our storytelling around this product." — The product needs a better pitch. Possibly also a better product.
terms.brolingo_tip: When someone says 'elevate,' ask where the ceiling is. Nobody ever specifies the ceiling.

terms.corporate_definition: The act of releasing a product, feature, or fix to users — used interchangeably whether it is complete, mostly complete, or actively on fire.
terms.real_definition: 'We shipped it' means it left the building. What condition it was in when it left — and what condition users find it in — are separate and often very different conversations. In modern software, 'shipped' is less a finish line and more a philosophical position: we have decided to let people encounter this now. Changes may continue. They probably will.
terms.example: "We shipped the new onboarding flow last night." — Three engineers are currently awake monitoring it.
terms.brolingo_tip: Ships also sink. Just saying.

terms.corporate_definition: A formal process of validating software behavior against expected outcomes prior to release.
terms.real_definition: Someone clicking the button to see if anything explodes. Often the last step, rarely given enough time, and frequently assigned to whoever looked up from their screen at the wrong moment. Also the word used when your buddy submits something through your contact form to see if it works. That is called 'manual QA' now. He can put it on his LinkedIn.
terms.example: "Did this go through testing?" — It went through someone's browser on their lunch break. The form submitted. That counts.
terms.brolingo_tip: Software testing exists on a spectrum from 'I clicked it once and it worked' to 'automated test suite covering 94% of edge cases.' Most shipped software is closer to the left side than anyone will admit in the post-mortem.

terms.corporate_definition: A software development approach in which the programmer, or anyone with $20 and wifi, describes their intent to an AI model, accepts the output, and ships before fully reading it.
terms.real_definition: Writing code by articulating vibes rather than syntax. You describe what you want — in plain English, with gestures if needed — and an AI produces something that works. The developer's role shifts from writing code to reviewing it, nudging it, and occasionally saying 'no, more like this.' Coined by Andrej Karpathy. Immediately embraced by everyone who ever wanted to build something but found semicolons unreasonably stressful.
terms.example: "I vibe coded the whole thing in a weekend." — This is either impressive or alarming, depending entirely on whether it's in production.
terms.brolingo_tip: Full disclosure: this website — a satirical dictionary mocking tech and corporate buzzwords — was itself built via vibe coding. Just look at all these dashes. We find this extremely funny. The owl has no notes.

terms.corporate_definition: To fully develop or expand upon a plan, idea, or strategy. [Note: this is not a real phrase. The expression you want is 'flesh out.']
terms.real_definition: The intended meaning is 'flesh out' — to add substance to something, as in putting flesh on a skeleton. 'Flush out' means to drive something from hiding using force, like flushing a bird from tall grass or clearing a drain. Both are, admittedly, unpleasant mental images. But only one of them applies to a strategic plan. The other turns your roadmap into a plumbing emergency. Choose your gross metaphor carefully.
terms.example: "We need to flush out the strategy before the board meeting." — The strategy will now be expelled from concealment by a surge of pressurized water. Or — and this is the move — you could flesh it out. Your call.
terms.brolingo_tip: Flesh out: add meat to bones (gross). Flush out: expel with force (also gross). One is correct here. The other is what you do to a clogged pipe. Neither phrase is pleasant, and yet here we are using both of them in a professional setting.
